item.title: 🟠 CrowdStrike’s AI SOC vision evolves as agentic uncertainty adds new twist
item.description:
Why this matters: Service impact is possible — verify vendor status before troubleshooting internally.

“The software we use has become an actor,” declared CrowdStrike President Michael Sentonas in his address on the dangers and opportunity of agentic AI at the company’s Fal.Con conference in September. It’s an idea that until recently would have been dismissed as absurd, yet across cybersecurity it’s now taken as a given.

For decades, the adversary has been nuisance hackers, professional cybercriminals, or well-resourced teams working for nation states. The arrival of rogue agents — underlined by real-world incidents such as OpenAI’s infamous assault on Hugging Face — has demolished this. Agents still work on behalf of humans, but they don’t always reason or act like them. They are entities with capabilities and an unpredictability unlike any threat businesses have ever faced.

item.title: 🟠 Barracuda’s security appliances have a security problem of their own
item.description:
Why this matters: Credential/phishing risk — reinforce MFA and watch for suspicious sign-ins.

Barracuda, which offers a wide variety of cybersecurity devices, has been bitten by a bug itself.

The company has disclosed two critical and high-severity vulnerabilities that, if chained together, could allow threat actors to bypass authorization controls and gain root access to devices.

They consist of a pre-authentication authorization bypass vulnerability, tracked as CVE-2026-116606 (rated a critical 9.3 severity on the common vulnerability scoring system), and a command injection vulnerability tracked as CVE-2026-111560 (rated an 8.6 high-severity on CVSS). Attackers need to have access to the admin interface of a susceptible device to successfully exploit these vulnerabilities.

Barracuda has released security patches, which it advises customers to apply immediately.

item.title: 🔴 Network appliances go more than a year without patches as exploits speed up
item.description:
Why this matters: Remote-code-execution risk — assess exposure and patch or mitigate quickly.

The median vulnerability on enterprise network appliances stays unpatched for more than a year, Microsoft’s own telemetry shows, even as the most damaging software flaws are being weaponized within days of disclosure.

Microsoft Security Research reported the findings Monday in an analysis of roughly 383,000 CVEs disclosed from 1999 through September 2026. It shows that the median time to patch a vulnerability exceeds a year for network appliances. The period is more than a month for Windows servers, over 10 weeks for Linux servers and applications running on macOS, and about two weeks for Windows workstations.

“That gap is the threat actor’s window, widest on the critical systems that stay exposed the longest,” Microsoft Security researchers Yair Tsarfaty and Or Begam wrote in a blog post detailing the findings. They were referring to the distance between how fast flaws are exploited and how slowly critical systems are patched.


Source: CSO Online  |  Severity: Critical  |  Age: 21h

A China-linked hacking group’s use of AI agents to identify security weaknesses during a global espionage campaign is raising concerns about whether enterprises can detect gaps in their defenses before automated attacks exploit them.

CrowdStrike reported that the group, tracked as VAPOR PANDA, used an AI-powered penetration testing framework called ARTEX to target more than 200 organizations worldwide over an 11-day period beginning October 17. The organizations included government agencies and businesses across at least 14 countries, with researchers confirming post-exploitation activity at nine.

At a global pharmaceutical company, the attackers instructed AI agents to examine running processes and folder listings on Windows machines to determine whether CrowdStrike’s Falcon sensor was installed, according to transcripts recovered by the cybersecurity firm.

Just a couple of weeks after a cyberattack on French supermarket refrigeration systems resulted in spoiled food, and even some fires, retailers in Belgium, Ireland, Sweden, Finland, and Estonia were hit with nearly-identical attacks on Monday.

The mid-October attack prompted an advisory from the French Computer Emergency Response Team (CERT-FR) recommending that organizations disconnect any refrigeration control systems with public IP addresses from the internet, and to reconnect them via a secure VPN only after verifying the configuration and, if necessary, restoring factory defaults.

In an emergency, the advisory suggested, organizations could simply filter connections to allow only the IP addresses of their refrigeration suppliers or service providers to connect, but this should not be a long-term solution.

item.description:

Cryptocurrency Exchange Binance blamed a compromised DevOps laptop for the loss of $6.3 billion in cryptocurrency last week, adding that it will now cover any losses faced by its customers.

“Binance will cover all losses from the Secure Assets Fund for Users (SAFU) and the company’s funds,” the world’s largest cryptocurrency exchange said in an update on Friday, adding that user funds are safe and that it had found no evidence of wallet private-key leakage during its investigation of the incident. It had frozen approximately $3 billion in assets on-chain, temporarily suspending withdrawals while security checks were completed, and revoking the affected address authorization.

“Between about 2:27am PT and 1:35pm PT today, a maliciously modified version of Anthropic’s Claude Code extension was made available in the Cursor VS Code Extension Marketplace,” Cursor said in a security notice.

Cursor removed the compromised versions, 2.1.312 and 2.1.313, after discovering they had been available in its VS Code extension marketplace for approximately 11 hours on October 29.

item.title: 🟠 Why do we keep testing employees for yesterday’s phishing attacks
item.description:
Why this matters: Credential/phishing risk — reinforce MFA and watch for suspicious sign-ins.

“Yesterday’s price is not today’s price,” a phrase Fat Joe popularized in 2021, reminds us that what worked yesterday may not deliver the same value today.

In cybersecurity, this matters when we continue to assess employees against familiar phishing techniques while attackers use AI to craft more convincing, personalized messages. Having conducted multiple phishing simulations and one in October, 2026, I believe we need to ask a harder question: are we preparing people for the phishing attacks they are likely to face today, or testing their ability to recognize or remember the warning signs we have taught them to expect? What happens when those warning signs don’t apply or they face novel attacks?

AI -enabled “phishing landscape”

Equifax CISO Jeremy Koppen sees the same dynamics most security chiefs are facing: hackers on the one side using AI to perform more sophisticated attacks at unprecedented speed, and defenders on the other adopting AI to match that volume and velocity.

“AI is changing the pace on both sides,” he says. “Attackers are using it to operate at greater scale, and Equifax is using it to innovate more quickly.”

In the next year, Koppen will continue to evolve Equifax’s security strategy to keep with an accelerating threat environment.

“That means building on the security already embedded across our design and development process, so checks run early and automatically,” he says. “It also means expanding how we use AI in our own security operations to handle routine work, so our experts can focus on the threats and initiatives that matter most. item.title: 🔵 Choosing a WAAP in 2026: 3 questions that separate the shortlist
item.description:
Why this matters: Potential budget or licensing impact — verify renewal terms and forecast changes.

One platform or four

Your WAF renewal is coming up. The API team has its own tooling in mind, the fraud team wants a bot product, and someone in networking owns DDoS. Four controls, four consoles, four sets of policies in front of the same applications. That is the situation a Web Application and API Protection platform, or WAAP, exists to replace: one service in front of the application portfolio that handles the WAF, API security, bot management, DDoS, and client-side script protection together.

The category is settled. What changed in 2026 is the evidence. Buyers now have certified test data that measures how well these platforms stop attacks and how often they stop legitimate traffic by mistake, and the two numbers together tell you more than any feature list.

item.description:

The identity landscape you’re responsible for looks nothing like it did just a few years ago. Employees and contractors now share the enterprise with service accounts, machine identities, and a fast-growing population of AI agents — all accessing business systems and data.

Every one of those identities represents an access decision, and every access decision is now a potential point of accountability that lands on your desk. Regulators and boards want proof. They expect security leaders to show who, or what, has access to critical systems and how that access is being governed.

But when human and nonhuman identities (NHIs) change faster than manual processes can keep up, proof becomes much harder to produce. item.title: 🔵 Why continuous governance, not periodic reviews, is the new standard for identity security
item.description:
Why this matters: Could affect sign-ins, MFA, or Conditional Access — watch for authentication issues.

Continuous identity governance is the operational model that enables organizations to validate access in real time, rather than relying on scheduled reviews to catch problems after they’ve already occurred. It replaces quarterly certifications and annual audits with ongoing visibility, automated policy enforcement, and always-current evidence of who, or what, has access to critical systems.

For CISOs, this shift matters now because the identity landscape has outgrown the tools built to govern it. Employees and contractors now share the environment with service accounts, machine identities, and autonomous AI agents, all requesting access at a pace no manual review cycle can track.  When governance happens only periodically, the gap between review dates becomes an exposure window that boards and regulators increasingly expect security leaders to own.

Why periodic reviews can’t keep up with modern identity environments

item.title: 🔴 Anthropic AI model finds Linux kernel bug that leads to remote root access
item.description:
Why this matters: Remote-code-execution risk — assess exposure and patch or mitigate quickly.

Linux servers running Multipath TCP (MPTCP) could be vulnerable to remote code execution through a flaw in the kernel’s networking stack.

Anthropic has disclosed a zero-click exploit developed with an unreleased Claude research model that allows an unauthenticated attacker to execute arbitrary commands as root, without requiring any user interaction.

Tracked as CVE-2026-98432, the vulnerability is a race-condition-induced use-after-free (UAF) bug in the Linux kernel. Anthropic demonstrated how an attacker could exploit the flaw remotely to leak kernel memory, defeat Kernel Address Space Layout Randomization (KASLR), hijack kernel control flow, and ultimately execute an attacker-controlled shell command.

A trillion-parameter AI model that its developer says could help attackers carry out real cyberattacks is now free to download, modify and run outside the developer’s control.

Mistral AI released the open weights of Mistral Large 4, which it calls “Le Chonk,” on Thursday, weeks after putting the multimodal model into public preview. The Paris-based company said it had monitored cybersecurity-related use of the preview in live traffic.

“Though we observed the model refusing to comply with black-box attacks against live targets, we see a potential for uplift to conduct real attacks,” the company wrote in a blog post announcing the release.

Mistral is modifying the model’s guardrails and will keep updating them in the coming months, the post added.
